text.p: Fishing boats carrying over 300 men reached safety six days after a cyclone ravaged southeast India's coastline, but almost 1,000 were still missing, Andhra Pradesh state officials said on Tuesday.
"315 fishermen have been found, 985 are still missing," Vijay Kumar, a senior official coordinating relief operations from the state capital in Hyderabad, told Reuters.
Before news that some boats had come ashore, the officials had said they feared the cyclone death toll could top 2,000.
The storm whipped up winds of 180 kmph (110 mph) and three metre (10 foot) high tidal waves that swept across coastal areas causing massive devastation last Wednesday night.
Kumar said that earlier reports from an Indian news agency that 1,000 men had been found were incorrect, but all hope of finding them had not yet been abandoned.
The missing fishermen set sail from the coast of East Godavari and West Godavari districts just before the cyclone zeroed in on their villages.
Hopes of finding them alive had been fading after air and sea searches failed to sight their boats.
At Etimoga village near the port town of Kakinada, the district headquarters of East Godavari, women and children waited in the hope that some 780 relatives had survived the cyclone and would return.
State Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu told a village gathering that helicopters and coast guards were making every effort to locate the missing men. The assurance had little effect on the crowd.
Malladi Dhanalaxi, 40, whose four brothers were among the missing, wept inconsolably.
"I don't think they will ever come back," she wailed.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda described the disaster in one of India's most prosperous farming areas as a national calamity.

Relief camps are sheltering 179,000 people whose homes have been destroyed or badly damaged, and medical teams are treating the injured, mostly for broken bones, and inoculating evacuees against waterborne diseases such as cholera.
Eric Jensen, of the Swiss-based International Committee of the Red Cross, surveyed the scene by helicopter on Tuesday, in response to requests for help from the Indian Red Cross.

"One positive thing I observed was that the water level had come down dramatically, close to normal," Jensen told Reuters. He added, though, that some of the outlying villages could only be reached by helicopter.
"The government and local population appear well organised, clearing roads and working to restore electricity," he said, adding that some normality was returning to the towns.
Jensen said relief workers were trying to provide adequate drinking water supplies as regular sources were contaminated, and there was always a fear of disease breaking out.
Officials said on Tuesday that so far no cases of cholera had been reported.
Gowda has called a meeting of officials of federal and state governments, banks and relief agencies for Wednesday to discuss ways of helping the cyclone victims.
The Andhra Pradesh state government has organised a relief fund.

The ICRC, meanwhile, has already released $200,000 worth of relief goods. And Jensen said he expected relief trucks to make the first deliveries of blankets, milk powder, tents and cooking oil on Thursday.
The latest estimate on losses to crops and property was 53.75 billion rupees ($1.5 billion).
Officials said the cyclone had affected nearly four million people out of a 10-million population in the two districts.
